speakers: Børge Brende (president and CEO, World Economic Forum)
Nicolai Tangen (CEO, Norges Bank Investment Management, interviewer)
summary: Interview of WEF president Børge Brende by NBIM CEO Nicolai Tangen on a fragmenting world order, resilient growth, the US, Europe and China, energy security and AI. Brende expects no full decoupling, more secure supply chains, high debt limiting fiscal response, and technology-driven productivity keeping growth from stagnating.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: we probably lose like four five trillion US dollars a year in cyber crime
claims.claim: Cyber crime costs about 4-5 trillion dollars a year (3-4% of global GDP), an area where even the US and China have overlapping interest in rules.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: between world orders, it's always uh unruly times
claims.claim: The post-1989 win-win order has been replaced by a competitive, more mercantilist one (soft power to hard power), and transitions between world orders are unruly.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: I think there is going to be a securing of the global value chains but I don't think there will be a full decoupling
claims.claim: Leaders want growth, and shoring that excludes the cheapest suppliers has an economic cost, so value chains will be secured but not fully decoupled.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: the fact that we have the highest global debt since 1945 also gives nation states um a harder time if we're going to see a recession
claims.claim: Record global debt leaves governments little fiscal muscle to respond to a recession.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: the new technologies will be the big game changer they will increase productivity maybe with 10% in the coming decade
claims.claim: New technologies could raise productivity by about 10% over the decade and offset slower trade growth, so the 1970s stagnation will not repeat.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: the way that trade was the engine of growth for decades grew two to three times more uh than trend growth
claims.claim: For decades trade grew two to three times faster than trend GDP and was the engine of growth, which decoupling removes.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: for decades we had a global trend growth of close to 4%. We are no more than we're closer to 3%
claims.claim: Global trend growth has fallen from about 4% to about 3%, not enough to meet development goals unless technology lifts it again.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: what we've seen so far on protectionist measures have not been so severe
claims.claim: Resilience reflects technology investment, post-Covid stimulus and protectionism so far not severe enough to hurt growth.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: if you are paying more for imports and you're creating also a tougher uh market at home when it comes to access to labor can lead to higher inflation
claims.claim: Tariffs raising import prices and immigration limits tightening labor access can raise US inflation.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: I believe more in the soft landing uh than in the hard landing
claims.claim: The US economy is solid and likely to keep growing, with soft landing more likely than hard.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: red tape uh bureaucracy um and uh so far not uh the most robust followup of the draggy report is holding Europe back
claims.claim: Red tape, weak follow-up of the Draghi report and internal political impulses hold Europe back, though sentiment has improved since Davos.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: look at the fastest growing of all the OCD economies including American economy is Spain
claims.claim: Spain is the fastest-growing OECD economy and Greece is growing fast too, after both were written off, and the euro remains the second reserve currency.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: it's gone down from 20% of their export in 2013 to now I think is
claims.claim: Chinese exports to the US fell from 20% of total in 2013 to about 11-12%, so China is more diversified; the US and China together are almost half of world GDP.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: we see that the demand has peaked we also know that the property prices. There is also a shrinking of the workforce
claims.claim: China faces structural challenges: peak demand for manufactured goods, property prices and a shrinking workforce, as global demand shifts to services and digital trade.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: being in power today is tough being in government there is anti-inccubent factor for those countries at least that do have uh these kind of elections
claims.claim: Shorter CEO and political tenures and an anti-incumbent factor encourage short-term thinking, though some reforms take a decade to pay off.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: having the leading global companies using their purchasing power to green their supply chain saying that for example Apple says that 25% of their aluminium needs to be green
claims.claim: Corporate purchasing commitments (Apple 25% green aluminium) create demand for green materials irrespective of legislation.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: We have seen in Europe uh how bad an idea it was to base uh almost half of our natural gas um from Russia
claims.claim: Energy security requires diversification: Europe's dependence on Russia for almost half its natural gas was costly, and the energy transition must not compromise security.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: looking at the gen AI I now can accelerate for example fusion uh nuclear uh that we thought was like maybe going to be available in three or four decades commercially
claims.claim: Gen AI could bring commercial fusion forward from three to four decades to maybe one decade.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: China is the first electrostate um a country that is basing a lot of their energy now on electricity
claims.claim: China bases more energy on electricity from renewables, balanced with coal, LNG and nuclear.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: had then a landish model that was developed for maybe one/ird one quarter of what others had done shows that we're maybe a little bit closer to the software phase
claims.claim: DeepSeek's model built for about a quarter of the cost suggests AI is closer to the software and applications phase than a hardware phase needing trillions in investment.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: if you increase productivity ity you can also increase prosperity but it also creates some fair of course fair for jobs
claims.claim: Gen AI will replace back-office jobs but, as agriculture fell from 95% to 2% of Swiss jobs, workers move up the value chain, raising productivity and prosperity.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: the country that's on top of the new technologies will probably emerge as the most powerful nation also of this century
claims.claim: Technology competition between China and the US will matter more than military competition, and others can enter.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: many of them did not exist two or three decades ago
claims.claim: Many of the 10 biggest companies did not exist two or three decades ago, so the next giants may not have started yet.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: Data is the new oxygen in this economy
claims.claim: Comparative advantage in AI comes from a large home market with data, capital, universities, R&D and engineers.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: in the platform economy the winner took it all
claims.claim: AI should reduce inequality in theory, but it needs education, energy and capital, and the platform economy shows winner-takes-all dynamics, though emerging economies with young populations get opportunities.

claims.speaker: Børge Brende
claims.quote: there is the jury is out uh if you need the huge trillion dollars u of investments
claims.claim: It is unclear whether AI requires trillions of dollars of investment, since good ideas have come from garages.
